title: Putting cyber risk in perspective, from the experts (our own CTO)
source: Axios — Putting cyber risk in perspective, from the experts (our own CTO) (2026-11-19)
body: Axios chief technology officer Dan Cox, who's spent 25 years at some of the world's biggest tech companies, puts the recent spate of high-profile failures in perspective: My parents, my siblings and plenty of other people are asking the same question: How worried should we be? The big picture: I've been in technology a long time. I take these threats seriously , but I'm not in panic mode. When something breaks, we need to understand what happened, how far it reaches and what we can do about it. A frightening headline doesn't answer those questions. Zoom out: The way I think about it, we've put powerful tools in more hands, and people are taking potshots to see what they can hit. Those shots can do real damage, and we need to protect ourselves. But hearing gunfire doesn't, by itself, mean an army is coming over the hill. We need to understand who's firing, what they can actually do and whether the threat is changing. Zoom in: Over the past few weeks, we've identified bad actors snooping around our own website, too. Our talented engineers have investigated threats and put mitigations in place. There may still be attempts on our site, but each incident gives us an opportunity to strengthen our systems. Between the lines: There are thousands of smart, resourceful and dedicated engineers working to protect the systems we all rely on. I see that commitment in our own team. I believe that if the threat grows, more people with those skills will step up. That's part of why I have confidence in our ability to respond, even as the threats evolve. The bottom line: Fred Rogers shared his mother's advice for frightening news: "Look for the helpers. You will always find people who are helping." I think about that here. There are a lot of capable people working on these problems. I have confidence in them, even while we have real work to do. I want people to feel informed enough to act, rather than frightened enough to assume the worst.
